notes:
Below are the notes, verse by verse. I used only the pages I actually read, and each point has its URL. My searches didn't turn up anything for some verses, and I couldn't read some kinds of sources at all. Those gaps are listed at the end.

---

**v. 27**
- **What Jesus showed them.** Barnes thinks Jesus corrected their idea of the Messiah. They expected a temporal prince; they were perplexed because Jesus had not assumed the regal power, but had been put to death. He showed them that according to the prophecies he ought to suffer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-27.htm
- **Gill's guesses at the passages.** Gill suggests Genesis 3:15 as the first prophecy. He adds the "types" (pictures) of Isaac and the bronze serpent, and the sacrifices in the Law of Moses. The same page quotes Matthew Henry: "A golden thread of gospel grace runs through the whole web of the Old Testament." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-27.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary.** It says the three groups named (Moses, the prophets, all the Scriptures) cover the whole Old Testament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-27.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed).** The verse shows how Christ is made known through the gospel, namely when light is thrown on the knowledge of him by the Law and the Prophets. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-27.html
- **Clarke.** He wishes the sermon had been kept. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-27.html
- **Constable.** He calls it a unique short course in Old Testament Christology, focused on passages about the Messiah's sufferings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-27.html
- **Desiring God (Baptist).** Luke keeps repeating "all" and "everything" (vv. 25, 27, 44). It reads this as Christ's claim that the whole Bible from beginning to end, is *about him*. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/taught-by-jesus

**vv. 28–29**
- I found no commentary on these verses in what I read.

**v. 30**
- **The four verbs.** A Bible Hub article notes that "took, blessed, broke, gave" appears almost verbatim in Luke 9:16 (feeding of the 5,000) and Luke 22:19 (Last Supper). By mirroring that pattern here, Luke signals continuity. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_is_Jesus_breaking_bread_important.htm
- **Jesus becomes the host.** Bible.org points out that they invited Him in as a guest, but He assumed the position of host and not just a guest. https://bible.org/article/christ-our-companion-luke-2413-35
- **Maclaren.** The hosts become the guests, and their table becomes His. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/luke/the-meal-at-emmaus.cfm
- **Was it the Lord's Supper? (the readings differ here)**
  - *Enduring Word (Guzik, Calvary Chapel / charismatic-leaning evangelical):* These two were not present at the last supper. Guzik quotes a writer who calls the meal in no sense a sacramental meal, as we use that word sacrament in our theology. It was a frugal supper in a village home. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
  - *Matthew Henry:* It was not a *miraculous* meal like that of the five loaves, nor a *sacramental* meal like that of the eucharist, but a *common* meal. He takes it as a lesson to ask a blessing at every meal. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-27.html
  - *Catholic (Catholic Answers):* The four verbs are liturgical language and particularly it's Eucharistic language. https://www.catholic.com/audio/sp/was-the-road-to-emmaus-a-mental-breakdown
  - *A side debate:* A Catholic article argues that the Emmaus bread was probably unleavened. It sets this against a common Orthodox argument for leavened bread in Communion. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/arguing-with-the-orthodox-about-bread

**v. 31**
- **Their eyes opened.** Guzik contrasts this with v. 16, where their eyes were "restrained." He lists Morrison's guesses at what gave Jesus away: His quiet majesty as host, the way He said the blessing, and The pierced hands that gave them the bread. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- **Maclaren.** We can't know exactly what triggered their recognition, or whether the earlier blindness was supernatural or their own fault. He thinks it was probably something in the Master's familiar way of breaking bread. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/luke/the-meal-at-emmaus.cfm
- **Got Questions.** Their physical eyes were held back, but their eyes of faith were being opened as Jesus opened the Scriptures to them. https://www.gotquestions.org/road-to-Emmaus.html

**v. 32**
- **Constable.** No wonder their hearts burned while Jesus explained the Scriptures. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-27.html
- **Clarke.** No wonder their hearts burned at such a *sermon*, from such a *preacher*. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-27.html

**vv. 33–34**
- Guzik places these verses under the heading "They tell the good news." My copy of his page broke off before his comments on them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- Got Questions notes that the passage adds evidence of another appearance and ties together the many eyewitnesses. https://www.gotquestions.org/road-to-Emmaus.html

**v. 35**
- **Protestant reading.** Bible Hub's study notes say the familiar act recalled His table fellowship and the Last Supper. The meal revealed the living Savior and pointed forward to the fellowship of believers who remember Christ's sacrificial death. https://biblehub.com/luke/24-35.htm
- **Catholic reading.** "The breaking of the bread" names the Eucharist (Acts 2:42, 46). Jesus being known "in" it shows that Jesus is really present in the Eucharist, not just a reminder of Him. https://www.catholic.com/audio/sp/was-the-road-to-emmaus-a-mental-breakdown

**vv. 36–38**
- **Matthew Henry.** The disciples were slow to believe at first and demanded full proof. That shows they believed only on the fullest demonstration of the thing that could be. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-39.html
- **Bridgeway.** Jesus appeared even though the doors were locked, so they thought He was a ghost who could pass through walls. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-39.html

**v. 39**
- **Calvin.** Jesus calls upon their bodily senses as witnesses, that they may not suppose that a shadow is exhibited to them instead of a body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-39.html
- **Gill.** The nail prints show He was raised in the same body in which He suffered. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-39.html
- **Barnes.** The words imply that a spirit can exist apart from the body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-39.htm
- **Ellicott.** There is a real corporeity, and yet there is a manifest exemption from the common conditions of corporeal existence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-39.htm
- **"Flesh and bones," not "flesh and blood."**
  - JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown) sees the same body living under different laws. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-39.htm
  - Cambridge warns that very precarious inferences have been drawn from leaving out "blood." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-39.htm
  - Guzik gives both views: perhaps a resurrection body has no blood, or perhaps Jesus simply named bones because you can feel them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-24/
- **The early "Docetism" heresy.** Light of Israel says Jesus was guarding against the later heresy that denied His real flesh. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-39.html
- **Catholic.** Catholic Answers says this verse alone disproves the idea that Jesus did not rise bodily. https://www.catholic.com/qa/was-jesus-resurrection-of-a-physical-or-purely-spiritual-nature
- **Desiring God (Baptist).** "Spiritual body" in 1 Corinthians 15 does not mean a body made of spirit: Body means corporeal: flesh and bones. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/meet-the-resurrected-you

**v. 40**
- **Pulpit Commentary.** The marks on His body let the frightened disciples see for sure that this was their Master. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-39.htm
- **Bible Hub study notes.** The wounds show that the resurrection did not erase the reality of His death. https://biblehub.com/luke/24-39.htm

**vv. 41–43**
- **Matthew Henry.** At Emmaus we aren't told that Jesus ate. Here He actually eats, so no one could object that His body wasn't truly alive again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-39.html
- **Bridgeway.** Eating showed His body had normal physical functions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-39.html

**v. 44**
- **Three-part Old Testament.** Law, Prophets and Psalms were the Jewish three-part division of the Old Testament. Barnes and Gill say "Psalms" stands for the whole "Writings" section, with the Psalms as its best-known book. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-44.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary.** "While I was still with you" shows that, in Jesus' mind, His time living among them was already over. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-44.htm
- **Matthew Henry.** *All things* must be fulfilled, even the *hardest,* even the *heaviest,* even the *vinegar*. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-44.html
- **Bible.org (Steven Cole).** "Must" is the same word as in vv. 7 and 26. It points to God's sovereign plan, so Jesus' death was no accident. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-116-our-mission-and-how-fulfill-it-luke-2444-49

**v. 45**
- **Bible.org (Cole).**
  - Opening their minds shows Christ's deity.
  - Even born-again disciples needed this before they could understand.
  - So believers must pray for God to open minds as they share the gospel.
  
  https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-116-our-mission-and-how-fulfill-it-luke-2444-49
- **Calvin.** He uses the same point: the apostles' minds were opened to understand the Scriptures, not to move beyond the Law and the Prophets. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-27.html

**vv. 46–47**
- **Bible.org (Cole).**
  - Christ's death was necessary for forgiveness.
  - "Beginning in Jerusalem," the city that had just killed its Messiah, shows no sinner is beyond saving.
  - "In His name" means by His authority.
  - "Nations" (Greek *ethnē*) supports the "people-group" approach to missions.
  
  https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-116-our-mission-and-how-fulfill-it-luke-2444-49
- **A debate about repentance.** Cole describes two views he calls inadequate. One says preaching repentance before faith adds works to salvation. The other says repentance just means changing your mind about who Jesus is. Cole, drawing on Spurgeon and J. C. Ryle, defines repentance as turning from sin to God, the "flip side" of saving faith, and a lifelong process. Same URL as above.

**v. 48**
- **Bible.org (Cole).** Witnesses don't invent a story. They tell what they saw, and that matched what God had already written. So the church is not free to change the message. Cole names Robert Schuller's self-esteem gospel as an example of a popular message that does this. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-116-our-mission-and-how-fulfill-it-luke-2444-49

**v. 49 (Protestant traditions really differ here)**
- **Common ground.** "The promise of My Father" is the Holy Spirit. "Clothed with power" means being equipped with divine strength for mission. https://biblehub.com/study/luke/24-49.htm
- **Pentecostal (Assemblies of God).** The AG position paper on Spirit baptism lists this verse under "Subsequence and Separability," meaning Spirit baptism is a separate experience after salvation. It says all believers should ardently expect and earnestly seek the promise of the Father, the baptism in the Holy Spirit and fire. It adds that with this baptism comes the enduement of power for life and service, the bestowment of the gifts. https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Baptism-in-the-Holy-Spirit
- **Non-Pentecostal evangelical (Bible.org, Cole).** The promise was fulfilled at Pentecost. Since then, everyone who repents and trusts Christ receives the Spirit at the moment of salvation. Believers must then learn to walk in the Spirit and not grieve or quench Him. Cole also sees the Trinity implied in the verse. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-116-our-mission-and-how-fulfill-it-luke-2444-49

**v. 50**
- **Timing (Ellicott).** On its own, Luke's account seems to put the Ascension about a day after the Resurrection. Ellicott answers that Luke himself recognises the forty days in Acts 1:3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-50.htm
- **Maclaren.**
  - Bethany was the home of so much of their friendship, which makes it a fitting place to say goodbye.
  - In the Gospel, Luke presents the Ascension as an ending and a farewell; in Acts, as a beginning.
  - He rejects the charge that the two accounts contradict each other.
  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-50.htm
- **Bengel.** The blessing belongs to all believers, because the Eleven stood for them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-50.htm
- **Lutheran (LCMS).** An LCMS article on recovering Ascension Day describes old images of Christ ascending with hands raised in blessing (citing this verse) and feet on the globe, showing His rule. https://witness.lcms.org/2022/recovering-ascension-day/
- **Desiring God (Piper).** The last thing Jesus says is a blessing. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-ascent-of-joy

**v. 51**
- **Textual note (Ellicott).** The words "and was carried up into heaven" are wanting in some of the best MSS., and are omitted accordingly by some recent editors. https://biblehub.com/luke/24-51.htm
- **Priestly blessing.** Bible Hub's notes link the raised hands to the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24–26. https://biblehub.com/luke/24-51.htm
- **Matthew Henry.** Jesus ascended not by force, but by his own act and deed. As he arose, so he ascended, by his own power. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/24-50.html
- **Maclaren.** He contrasts Elijah's whirlwind and fiery chariot with Christ's calm rising. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-50.htm

**vv. 52–53**
- **Maclaren.** Their "great joy" is a riddle that points ahead to Acts, where the Ascension is a beginning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-50.htm
- **Benson.** "Continually in the temple" means they attended at the hours of service. They praised God for sending the Messiah, raising Him, and taking Him up to heaven. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/24-50.htm
- **Bible Hub study notes.** Their worship and joy show they saw His leaving as victory, not loss. https://biblehub.com/luke/24-51.htm

---

**Gaps (left out because I didn't find them):**
- **Missing sources:** no netbible.org notes, Bible Odyssey articles, Orthodox (oca.org) material, or Methodist/Wesleyan commentary.
- **Missing debated teaching:** nothing on prosperity, Word of Faith or hyper-grace readings. The only popular-teaching critique I found is Cole's comment on Schuller (v. 48).
- **Missing verses:** nothing for vv. 28–29. Coverage of vv. 33–34 and 36–38 is thin.
- **Enduring Word:** my copy of the page cut off partway through the chapter. Some Guzik points above come only from search-result excerpts of that page.
